Queenslander: Reopen the Records · Section 1, The Station · The Count

What do the registers tell us about Hannah Rigby, James Davis and John Baker, and what years of their lives did they never record?

Listen: the evidence (about 2 min, synthetic Australian voice)
Transcript

The Count. A reading from the file.

Moreton Bay was established in 1824 as a place of secondary punishment, for men and women already under sentence in New South Wales.

Hannah Rigby, a seamstress from Liverpool, was convicted of larceny in 1821 and transported. She received two further colonial sentences and was sent to Moreton Bay. Hospital records show one of her young sons was treated for fever after her arrival. When the station closed, she was allowed to remain, as servant to the medical officer, David Ballow. In 1840 her residual sentence was remitted. She stayed. In October 1853 she was found dead in her hut near Queen Street. The inquest returned a verdict of death by the visitation of God.

James Davis, a blacksmith's son from Glasgow, arrived at the station on the eighteenth of February 1829, and absconded six weeks later. He was taken in by Kabi Kabi people of the Wide Bay, and lived among them for thirteen or fourteen years. In May 1842, Andrew Petrie's party found him.

John Sterry Baker absconded in January 1826. He lived with people of the Upper Brisbane for fourteen years and nine months. In August 1840 he walked back into the nearly emptied station, and surrendered.

The same pages that list the living list the dead. William Parfitt, October 1828. John Carroll and Michael Condron, February 1829. Matthew Gallagher, January 1832.

The returns recorded names, trades, arrivals, deaths, abscondings, and residual sentences. The registers recorded the absconding, and the return. Weigh the documents. The pages remain open.

Exhibits

Chronological Register of Convicts at Moreton Bay
1824–1839 · Queensland State Archives, ITM869689

Records: names, arrivals, abscondings, returns and sentences of those held at the station.

Does not record: the years a man spent outside the boundary, or what those years were.

Particulars of the Colonial Sentence of Hannah Rigby, with covering letter
4 July 1840 · State Library of Queensland, Colonial Secretary’s Correspondence 33054-003265 (FromThePage)

Records: ship, trial, offence, sentence, arrival at Moreton Bay, and the order to remit the remainder.

Does not record: what the residual years felt like, or her own words.

“Wild White Men” (Davis / Petrie recollections)
30 December 1913 · Trove, article 111218390

Records: a later published recollection of men who lived for years among Aboriginal people.

Does not record: the accounts of the Kabi Kabi and Upper Brisbane people who took them in.

What the file doesn’t hold

The thirteen, fourteen years lived outside the boundary: the registers mark the absconding and the return, and nothing in between.
